Marathon Petroleum has fallen roughly 4.4% over the past week, tracking a sharp decline from its October 16 peak of $478. The immediate backdrop is geopolitical tension in the Middle East—Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and drone/missile interceptions—which pushed Brent crude to $116 earlier this week. While that might seem bullish for a refiner, what likely weighs on MPC is the pattern underneath: oil prices have climbed steadily (Brent now at $115.22 globally, WTI at $107.89 domestically) but refinery utilization is already running at a high 93.4%, leaving little room for margin expansion even as input costs rise.

The broader pressure is that refiners profit most when crude is cheap and demand is strong. Rising geopolitical oil premiums—driven by Iran tensions and Houthi attacks—boost crude prices but don't automatically boost the refined products (gasoline, diesel) that refiners sell, squeezing the profit spread between input and output. Gasoline and diesel inventories remain elevated, which also softens pricing power on the output side.
